arXiv:2604.18312v1 [cs.LG] 20 Apr 2026

Scale-free adaptive planning for deterministic dynamics & discounted rewards

Peter L. Bartlett​ Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley, USA    Victor Gabillon​ Affiliation: Noah’s Ark Lab, Huawei Technologies, London, UK    Jennifer Healey​ Affiliation: Adobe Research, San Jose, USA    Michal Valko​ Affiliation: SequeL team, INRIA Lille - Nord Europe, France Correspondence to: victor.gabillon@huawei.com
Abstract

We address the problem of planning in an environment with deterministic dynamics and stochastic discounted rewards under a limited numerical budget where the ranges of both rewards and noise are unknown. We introduce PlaTγ\gammaPOOS, an adaptive, robust, and efficient alternative to the OLOP (open-loop optimistic planning) algorithm. Whereas OLOP requires a priori knowledge of the ranges of both rewards and noise, PlaTγ\gammaPOOS dynamically adapts its behavior to both. This allows PlaTγ\gammaPOOS to be immune to two vulnerabilities of OLOP: failure when given underestimated ranges of noise and rewards and inefficiency when these are overestimated. PlaTγ\gammaPOOS additionally adapts to the global smoothness of the value function. PlaTγ\gammaPOOS acts in a provably more efficient manner vs. OLOP when OLOP is given an overestimated reward and show that in the case of no noise, PlaTγ\gammaPOOS learns exponentially faster.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

We consider the problem of planning in a general stochastic environment with deterministic dynamics and discounted rewards. Our goal is to recommend the best first action for an agent to take from a given state. We envision that the discount factor γ\gamma is known and that our learner has a limited allocation of nn interactions to spend querying a generative model of the environment. The objective is to maximize the sum of discounted rewards of the best sequence of actions following from the recommended first action. This is equivalent to minimizing the simple regret. We introduce the algorithm PlaTγ\gammaPOOS, Planning wiTh γ\gamma Plus an Online Optimization Strategy, as a robust and efficient scale-free alternative to the OLOP algorithm (open-loop optimistic planning, Bubeck & Munos, 2010; Leurent & Maillard, 2019) for this setting. Our algorithm implements a scale-free function optimization strategy similar to SequOOL (Bartlett et al., 2019) rather than an upper-confidence-bound approach which allows us to efficiently adapt to the problem space without prior knowledge of the ranges of the noise or the rewards.

Planning in a stochastic environment is an important setting often modeled by Markov decision processes (MDPs, Puterman, 1994; Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis, 1996). One approach to solving these settings is to find the optimal policy that maximizes the expected sum of rewards and then generate an action recommendation according to that optimal policy. Unfortunately, in most practical settings where we are limited by computational resources, finding this optimal policy is often not possible, especially when the state space becomes large. Therefore, instead of trying to estimate the optimal policy of the MDP, we focus only on finding the best first action given our budget. We evaluate the performance of the recommendation in terms of the simple regret, the difference in reward between choosing the optimal first action vs. choosing our recommended first action and then in both cases choosing an optimal sequence of actions following the first action. This metric is often used to evaluate planning strategies that optimize numeric budgets (Bubeck & Munos, 2010; Buşoniu & Munos, 2012; Grill et al., 2016), in contrast to the cumulative regret where we are penalized during the search for querying sub-optimal actions. Once the agent takes the first action and moves to the next state, our evaluation can be repeated with a new budget allocation and the following best first action can be recommended. This allows us to approximately follow an optimal policy, action by action, in an online way. Previously, there have been several strategies proposed on how to efficiently allocate a numeric budget to search for an optimal value in a stochastic space. Many of these have been successfully implemented using methods based on upper confidence bounds (UCBs) such as UCT (Upper Confidence Trees, Kocsis & Szepesvári, 2006). This approach has been proven to be very efficient in practice (Coulom, 2007; Gelly et al., 2006; Silver et al., 2016), however, UCT can badly misbehave on some problems (Coquelin & Munos, 2007) and more theoretically sound approaches have been proposed (Hren & Munos, 2008; Bubeck & Munos, 2010; Buşoniu & Munos, 2012; Feldman & Domshlak, 2014; Szörényi et al., 2014; Kaufmann & Koolen, 2017; Shah et al., 2019). Some of these methods are connected to the ones from function optimization (Bubeck et al., 2011; Munos, 2011; Valko et al., 2013) as shown by Munos (2014), however, one key difference is that in planning, as opposed to function optimization, the structure of the reward is a discounted reward, specifically a sum of rewards discounted by factor γ\gamma. This reward structure influences the behavior of the optimizers (Bubeck & Munos, 2010), in particular, the discount factor brings smoothness to the value function which in turn makes it easier to optimize. PlaTγ\gammaPOOS exploits the effect of the discount factor to efficiently manage an adaptive planning strategy in the face of unknown ranges of noise and rewards.

This adaptive strategy of PlaTγ\gammaPOOS makes it more robust and efficient in practice than other planning strategies. For example, even though they are theoretically sound, the empirical performance of UCB-based approaches depends on the careful tuning of the upper confidence bound. If the upper confidence bound is too large then the UCB-based learner plays very conservatively by overestimating suboptimal options for many rounds. Moreover, these UCBs might depend on instance parameters that are simply not known such as the range of the rewards and the range of the noise. We build on the function optimization approach of Bartlett et al. (2019) that does not use UCBs and obtains improved results over the state-of-the-art by adapting to the problem difficulty with a scale-free approach. PlaTγ\gammaPOOS adapts this scale-free optimization to planning. This scale-free property becomes a desired feature as machine learning gets closer to applications, whether it is online (Ross et al., 2013; Orabona & Pál, 2018) or deep learning (Orabona & Tommasi, 2017), since many parameters are never known.

In terms of planning strategy, the PlaTγ\gammaPOOS algorithm is an adaptive, robust, and efficient alternative to OLOP. Whereas OLOP requires the knowledge of where the ranges of both rewards and noise, PlaTγ\gammaPOOS dynamically adapts its behavior to the both ranges, as well as some potential additional global smoothness of the value function. Our algorithm’s ability to adapt allows it to avoid failure in cases where the ranges of noise and rewards are underestimated and to act more efficiently in cases where they are overestimated. PlaTγ\gammaPOOS recovers the results of OLOP while allowing improvements in various classes of problems.

Our contributions

We show that PlaTγ\gammaPOOS

  • •

    adapts its behavior to an unknown range of rewards,

  • •

    requires no apriori assumptions or knowledge on noise,

  • •

    empirically learns much faster than UCB approaches,

  • •

    gets the fast rate of deterministic planning in low noise for all regime; in particular, it learns exponentially faster than OLOP when there happens to be no noise,

  • •

    adapts also the global smoothness ρ\rho and ν\nu beyond the base smoothness provided by γ\gamma.

We additionally address a realistic constraint where the agent can only reset to the original state and not to any state it wishes. Our results hold for MDPs with deterministic dynamics and can equally be applied to open loop planning problems (as discussed by Munos 2014) where we search for the best sequence of actions, ignoring the actual states that are reached after each action (Bubeck & Munos, 2010).

Related algorithms, where the objective is to find the value of the state rather than to identify the best action, include TrailBlazer (Grill et al., 2016) and StOP (Szörényi et al., 2014). A key difference is that these algorithms are fixed confidence and output a value using a small number of samples given an accuracy/probability, whereas our algorithm does exploration under a fixed budget of samples and guarantees how good the found action is. Even for simple multi-arm bandits, these two problems have different complexity (Carpentier & Locatelli, 2016) and can only be equivalent under unrealistic side knowledge (Gabillon et al., 2012). These related algorithms are also impractical for our setting. TrailBlazer uses confidence bounds that are humongous and StOP takes exponential time. Similar to OLOP, both also need to know noise and reward ranges.

2.1 Optimistic planning under finite numerical budget

We assume that we have a generative model of ff and rr that generates simulated transitions and rewards. We want to make the best possible use of this model in order to recommend a best next action a⁡(n)a(n) such that the sum of the rewards resulting from playing a⁡(n)a(n) and then optimally afterwards is as close as possible to playing optimally from the beginning. For that purpose, we define the performance loss that we aim to minimize rnr_{n} as

rn≜maxa∈A⁡Q⋆​(x,a)−Q⋆​(x,a⁡(n)).r_{n}\triangleq\max_{a\in A}Q^{\star}\left(x,a\right)-Q^{\star}\left(x,a\left(n\right)\right).

3 Optimization vs. planning

Our PlaTγ\gammaPOOS approach is a very close sibling to the flat optimization algorithm, StroquOOL (Bartlett et al., 2019), however, we explain how the structure of the planning setting and the discount factor γ\gamma shaped our approach. The optimal application of an optimization algorithm to the planning setting is not straightforward as discussed by Bubeck & Munos (2010). In their Section 2.2, Bubeck & Munos (2010) show that optimization can be applied to the planning problem either in a naïve way or a good way. The authors take as an example the uniform planning problem. The naïve and good strategies are evaluated by comparing the uncertainty |u​(a)−u^​(a)||u(a)-\widehat{u}(a)| of their estimates u^​(a)\widehat{u}(a). Both strategies collect rewards identically, evaluating u⁡(a)u(a) for all the KHK^{H} nodes a∈AHa\in A^{H} at a fixed depth H≜h⁡(a)H\triangleq h(a) by allocating one episode (of length HH) for each aa and receiving rh,ar_{h,a}, 1≤h≤H1\leq h\leq H. In the naïve version, for all sequences aa, the estimation of u⁡(a)u(a) uses only the HH samples collected in the one episode related to aa. Here u^​(a)≜∑h=00​p​t​(a)−1γt​rh,a\widehat{u}(a)\triangleq\sum^{0pt(a)-1}_{h=0}\gamma^{t}r_{h,a} and Ta[h]=1T_{a_{[h]}}=1. In contrast, the good planning strategy reuses estimates. For two distinct sequences aa and a′a^{\prime}, the good strategy reuses any sample of rh,ar_{h,a} it gets for the estimation of both u⁡(a)u(a) and u⁡(a′)u(a^{\prime}) if a[h]=a[h]′a_{[h]}=a^{\prime}_{[h]}. In this case, u^(a)≜∑h=00​p​t​(a)−1γt1KH−h∑a′:a[h]=a[h]′rh,a′\widehat{u}(a)\triangleq\sum^{0pt(a)-1}_{h=0}\gamma^{t}\frac{1}{K^{H-h}}\sum_{a^{\prime}:a_{[h]}=a^{\prime}_{[h]}}r_{h,a^{\prime}} and Ta[h]=KH−hT_{a_{[h]}}=K^{H-h}. This comparison is used to demonstrate the advantage of the use of the cross-sequence information to concentrate the estimate of the mean reward associated with each action more efficiently. It is by using this type of cross-sequence information that OLOP is able to obtain a reduced regret over a naïve application of HOO for optimization (Bubeck et al., 2011) to the planning problem.

The previous discussion on cross-sequence information is tied to the case of uniform exploration strategies. Good uniform strategies guarantee Ta[h]=KHu−hT_{a_{[h]}}=K^{H_{u}-h} by exploring until a reasonably shallow depth HuH_{u} but sampling all KHuK^{H_{u}} nodes and sharing cross sequence information. In the case of OLOP, HOO, or, particularly StroquOOL, only a subset SS of size |S|≪KHu|S|\ll K^{H_{u}} of the most promising nodes are explored but at a deeper depth Hs≫HuH_{s}\gg H_{u}. Therefore, obtaining a lower bound on the number of sequence of actions at depth HsH_{s} that contains aa for a given sub-sequence of actions aa at depth h<Hsh<H_{s} is complex in general. Actually one can design a problem with two actions that would drastically limit the amount of cross-sequence information for the optimal sequence of actions a⋆a^{\star} in StroquOOL. As a result, applying StroquOOL with information sharing may not be enough and we chose to algorithmically ensure hat a node at depth h+1h+1 will be pulled γ2\gamma^{2} times less than a node at depth hh. Indeed, using Chernoff-Hoeffding inequalities, we have |u⁡(a)−u^​(a)|≤∑h=0h⁡(a)−1γh/Ta[h]|u(a)-\widehat{u}(a)|\leq\sum_{h=0}^{h(a)-1}\gamma^{h}/\sqrt{T_{a_{[h]}}}. However, PlaTγ\gammaPOOS, through some simple reparametrization, remains very close to StroquOOL and we leave as an open question whether equivalent theoretical guarantees could be proved directly for StroquOOL applied to planning.

4 Deterministic dynamics and rewards

In this section, we consider a simpler case of deterministic rewards in order to introduce our new ideas. The evaluations are noiseless, that is ∀t\forall t, εt≜0\varepsilon_{t}\triangleq 0 and rt≜r⁡(xt,at)r_{t}\triangleq r(x_{t},a_{t}).

In Figure 1, we provide the SequOOL (Bartlett et al., 2019) algorithm applied to planning. In this case, it is straightforward to follow the analysis of SequOOL in order to obtain the same rates of simple regret as the state of the art algorithm OPD for the doubly deterministic case (Hren & Munos, 2008; Munos, 2014), up to logarithmic factors; and get the result11 1 log¯​(n)\overline{\log}(n) is the nn-th harmonic number of Theorem 1. This direct usage was already discussed by Munos (2014, Section 5.1). Using SequOOL for planning already permits to have an algorithm that does not use the parameter RmaxR_{\max} and that adapts to extra smoothness in the value function ν\nu, ρ\rho as discussed Section 2. Note that to obtain similar adaptations to RmaxR_{\max}, ν,\nu, and ρ,\rho, we could have already used SOO (Munos, 2014). However, SOO does not come with optimal simple regret (Bartlett et al., 2019).

Theorem 1.

For any planning problem with associated (ν,ρ)(\nu,\rho), and branching factor κ≜κu​(ν,ρ)\kappa\triangleq\kappa^{u}(\nu,\rho), the simple regret of SequOOL is after nn rounds bounded as follows.

  1. •

    If κ=1\kappa=1, thenrn≤ν​ρ1C​⌊nlog¯​n⌋.\>r_{n}\leq\ \nu\rho^{\frac{1}{C}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{\overline{\log}\,n}\right\rfloor}.

  2. •

    If κ>1\kappa>1, then rn=𝒪⁡(ν​(log⁡κC​⌊nlog¯​n⌋)−log⁡1/ρlog⁡κ).\>r_{n}=\mathcal{O}\left(\nu\left(\frac{\log{\kappa}}{C}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{\overline{\log}\,n}\right\rfloor\right)^{-\frac{\log{1/\rho}}{\log{\kappa}}}\right)\!.

On the reset condition

In practice, physical constraints can force the exploration to interact with the unknown environment under a reset condition. This means that there exists a starting state xx and a trajectory needs to start from this state and following a given policy. Therefore, if we wish to collect a sample from an arbitrary state x′x^{\prime} after a reset, we must first reach that state from the starting state xx.

SequOOL is a strategy that explores the MDP deeper and deeper from an initial starting state xx. The original SequOOL strategy did not consider any reset condition, so to make a comparable analysis we will say that to ‘open’ a node aa you first need to reach aa at a budget cost of h⁡(a)h(a) which is equal to the depth of aa. This additional cost has the consequence that SequOOL with reset will not be able to explore as deeply as without. A naïve extension is shown in Figure 2. Under a total limited budget of nn, the number of nodes now open at depth hh is 𝒪⁡(n/h2)\mathcal{O}(n/h^{2}) instead of 𝒪⁡(n/h)\mathcal{O}(n/h) and the maximal depth is now of order of n\sqrt{n} instead of nn. However, this does not influence the simple regret when κ>1\kappa>1 by more than numerical constants as shown in Theorem 2. When κ>1\kappa>1, the exponentially diminishing simple regret remains but is changed from ρn\rho^{n} to ρn\rho^{\sqrt{n}}.

Theorem 2.

For a planning problem with associated (ν,ρ)(\nu,\rho), and branching factor κ≜κu​(ν,ρ)\kappa\triangleq\kappa^{u}(\nu,\rho), after nn rounds, the simple regret of SequOOL with reset condition verifies:

  1. •

    If κ=1\kappa=1, thenrn≤ν​ρ1C​⌊nlog¯​n⌋.\>r_{n}\leq\ \nu\rho^{\sqrt{\frac{1}{C}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{\overline{\log}\,n}\right\rfloor}}.

  2. •

    If κ>1\kappa>1, then rn≤𝒪⁡(ν​(log⁡κC​⌊nlog¯​n⌋)−log⁡1/ρlog⁡κ)\>r_{n}\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\nu\left(\frac{\log{\kappa}}{C}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{\overline{\log}\,n}\right\rfloor\right)^{-\frac{\log{1/\rho}}{\log{\kappa}}}\right).

5 Deterministic dynamics, stochastic rewards

We now describe the PlaTγ\gammaPOOS algorithm detailed in Figure 3. In the presence of noise, it is natural to evaluate the cells multiple times, not just one time as in the deterministic case. The amount of times a cell should be evaluated to differentiate its value from the optimal value of the function depends on the gap between these two values as well as the range of noise. As we do not want to make any assumptions on knowing these quantities, our algorithm tries to be robust to any potential values by not making a fixed choice on the number of evaluations. Intuitively, we do this following a path similar to StroquOOL (Bartlett et al., 2019) by using a modified version of SequOOL, denoted SequOOL(m),(m), that allows us to evaluate cells mm times, whereas for SequOOL, m=1m=1. Evaluating cells more times (mm large) leads to a better quality of the mean estimates in each cell, however, as a trade-off, it uses more evaluations per depth. This would normally limit us from exploring deep depths of the partition, however, PlaTγ\gammaPOOS takes advantage of the knowledge of γ\gamma which gives less weight to reward collected deeper in the tree. In order to obtain the concentration results for a node aa on u^​(a)−u​(a)\widehat{u}(a)-u(a) in Lemma 2, PlaTγ\gammaPOOS uses a Chernoff-Hoeffding result that gives with high probability, u^​(a)−u⁡(a)≤∑h=0h⁡(a)−1γ2​h/Ta[h]\widehat{u}(a)-u(a)\leq\sqrt{\sum_{h=0}^{h(a)-1}\gamma^{2h}/T_{a_{[h]}}} and balances the range of confidence intervals at different depths. Therefore, PlaTγ\gammaPOOS tends to pull less with deeper depth as the number of pulls for a fixed mm is ⌈h​m​γ2​h⌉\left\lceil hm\gamma^{2h}\right\rceil where the additional hh factor ensures that the sum of confidence interval until depth hh is bounded for any hh. PlaTγ\gammaPOOS then implicitly performs log⁡n\log n instances of SequOOL(m)(m) each with a number of evaluations of m=2pm=2^{p}, where p∈[0:logn]p\in[0:\log n].

In Figure 3, remember that ‘opening’ a node means ‘evaluating’ its children actions. The algorithm opens nodes by sequentially diving them deeper and deeper from the root node h=0h=0 to a maximal depth of hmaxh_{\rm max}. At depth hh, we allocate, in an almost decreasing fashion, different number of evaluations ⌈h​2p​γ2​h⌉\left\lceil h2^{p}\gamma^{2h}\right\rceil to the nodes with highest value of that depth, with pp starting at ⌊log2⁡(hmax/h)⌋\left\lfloor\log_{2}(h_{\rm max}/h)\right\rfloor down to 00. The best node that has been evaluated at least 𝒪⁡(hmax/h)\mathcal{O}(h_{\rm max}/h) times is opened with 𝒪⁡(hmax/h)\mathcal{O}(h_{\rm max}/h) evaluations, the two next best cells that have been evaluated at least 𝒪⁡(hmax/(2​h)CLOSE\mathcal{O}(h_{\rm max}/(2h) times are opened with 𝒪⁡(hmax/(2​h))\mathcal{O}(h_{\rm max}/(2h)) evaluations, the four next best cells that have been evaluated at least 𝒪⁡(hmax/(4​h))\mathcal{O}(h_{\rm max}/(4h)) times are opened with 𝒪⁡(hmax/(4​h))\mathcal{O}(h_{\rm max}/(4h)) evaluations and so on, until some 𝒪⁡(hmax/h)\mathcal{O}(h_{\rm max}/h) next best cells that have been evaluated at least once are opened with one evaluation. More precisely, given, pp and hh, we open, with ⌈h​2p​γ2​h⌉\left\lceil h2^{p}\gamma^{2h}\right\rceil evaluations, the ⌊hmax/(h⁡⌈h​2p​γ2​h⌉)⌋\left\lfloor h_{\rm max}/(h\left\lceil h2^{p}\gamma^{2h}\right\rceil)\right\rfloor non-previously-opened nodes ah,i∈Aha^{h,i}\in A^{h} with highest values u^​(ah,i)\widehat{u}(a^{h,i}) and given that Tah,i≥⌈(h−1)​2p​γ2​(h−1)⌉T_{a^{h,i}}\geq\left\lceil(h-1)2^{p}\gamma^{2(h-1)}\right\rceil. The maximum number of evaluations of any node is 2pmax2^{p_{\rm max}}, with 2pmax=𝒪⁡(hmax)2^{p_{\rm max}}=\mathcal{O}(h_{\rm max}) as pmax≜⌊log2⁡(hmax)⌋p_{\rm max}\triangleq\left\lfloor\log_{2}\left(h_{\rm max}\right)\right\rfloor. For each p∈[0:pmax]p\in[0:p_{\rm max}], the candidate output apa^{p} is the node aa with the highest estimated value such that all actions leading to that node have been evaluated in the following way ∀t∈[2:0pt(a)],Ta[t]≥⌈(t−1)2pγ2​(t−1)⌉\forall t\in[2:0pt(a)],T_{a_{[t]}}\geq\left\lceil(t-1)2^{p}\gamma^{2(t-1)}\right\rceil. We set hmax≜⌊n/(2​(log2⁡n+1)2)⌋.h_{\rm max}\triangleq\left\lfloor n/(2(\log_{2}n+1)^{2})\right\rfloor\!.

Worst-case comparison with OLOP when bb is large and known

In Table 1, we give our results for various classes of problems depending on the whether γ2​κ≥1\gamma^{2}\kappa\geq 1, whether κ=1\kappa=1 or κ>1\kappa>1, and several conditions for the range of the noise bb. The results for OLOP were distinguishing the results based on γ2​κ\gamma^{2}\kappa being greater or smaller than 11. For these two cases, we recover the same rate in term of nn for the simple regret, as displayed in Table 1 with a grey background color, for instance taking b=1b=1 like in OLOP and having ρ=γ.\rho=\gamma. However, we provide more specific treatment for sub-cases with associated improvements that we list and detail next.

Adaptation to the range of the noise bb without a prior knowledge

Our analysis shows that PlaTγ\gammaPOOS adapts favorably to the unknown range of noise. Already, in the standard cases discussed above, where the noise is large, our bound already adapts to the amount of noise as it scales with n/b2n/b^{2}. OLOP requires an estimate b~\widetilde{b} of bb and has a regret scaling with n/b~2n/\widetilde{b}^{2} which is problematic in case of a wrong estimate b~≫b\widetilde{b}\gg b. Moreover, we give technical conditions on the range of noise that shows when PlaTγ\gammaPOOS gets improved rates. When γ2​κ≥1\gamma^{2}\kappa\geq 1, OLOP was already obtaining rates that were the same as the rates of deterministic reward case. Therefore, beyond the n/b2n/b^{2} improvement and the adaptation to extra smoothness that will be discussed latter, no more rate improvement should be expected. In the case γ2​κ≤1\gamma^{2}\kappa\leq 1, the improvement are even more striking. When the noise is very low, then contrary to the OLOP rate of 𝒪⁡(1/n)\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{n}), we obtain the deterministic rate of OPD (Hren & Munos, 2008; Munos, 2014) which is either n−log(1/ρ)/logκn^{-\log(1/\rho)/\log\kappa} or ρn\rho^{n}. These improved rates could not be obtained by OLOP. Indeed, OLOP relies on upper confidence bound (UCB) that uses a range of the noise b~\widetilde{b} as input,

u¯(a)=𝒪(u^(a)+∑h=0h⁡(a)−1γhb~1Ta[a]+Rmax​γh⁡(a)1−γ)⋅\overline{u}(a)=\mathcal{O}\left(\widehat{u}(a)+\sum_{h=0}^{h(a)-1}\gamma^{h}\widetilde{b}\sqrt{\frac{1}{T_{a_{[a]}}}}+\frac{R_{\max}\gamma^{h(a)}}{1-\gamma}\right)\!\cdot

This works if b~=b\widetilde{b}=b. However, the true bb is unknown. If b=0b=0, using any b~>0\widetilde{b}>0 will not result in an improved rate.

Adaptation to additional smoothness ν\nu and ρ\rho beyond γ\gamma

As defined in Section 2, we aim to adapt to the true smoothness ν,ρ\nu,\rho of VV which can go beyond γ\gamma. We show that PlaTγ\gammaPOOS is able to take advantage of ν,ρ\nu,\rho in a large portion of cases. In most cases, the rate γ\gamma in OLOP is replaced by ρ\rho in PlaTγ\gammaPOOS. In the case where γ2​κ≥1\gamma^{2}\kappa\geq 1 we have

rOLOP=𝒪⁡(n−log⁡(1/γ)log⁡(κ))≤𝒪⁡(n−log⁡(1/ρ)log⁡(γ2​κ/ρ2))=rPlaTγPOOS.r^{\texttt{OLOP}}=\mathcal{O}(n^{-\frac{\log(1/\gamma)}{\log(\kappa)}})\leq\mathcal{O}(n^{-\frac{\log(1/\rho)}{\log(\gamma^{2}\kappa/\rho^{2})}})=r^{{\texttt{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.2,0}PlaT$\gamma$POOS}}}}.

Adaptation to the deterministic case and κ=1\kappa=1

PlaTγ\gammaPOOS adapts to the branching factor κ\kappa of the problem that under low noise conditions, leads to an exponentially decreasing simple regret rnPlaTγPOOS=𝒪⁡(ν​ρn).r_{n}^{{\texttt{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.2,0}PlaT$\gamma$POOS}}}}=\mathcal{O}(\nu\rho^{\sqrt{n}}). This is a light-years improvement over OLOP for these conditions, as OLOP’s regret is at best rnPlaTγPOOS=𝒪(n−1/2)r_{n}^{{\texttt{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.2,0}PlaT$\gamma$POOS}}}}=\mathcal{O}(n^{-1/2}). This result is possible because PlaTγ\gammaPOOS explores much deeper than OLOP, as its maximal depth is of order nn. Actually, in most scenarios, the actual larger depth explored will be of order n\sqrt{n} due to sampling limitations. On the other hand, OLOP can only go log⁡n\log n deep.

Moreover, κ=1\kappa=1 is a common case in planning. Indeed, as discussed by Bubeck & Munos (2010), κ=1\kappa=1 is equivalent to having near-optimal dimension d=0d=0 in an optimization task (Munos, 2014) which is a common value as shown by Valko et al. (2013). Therefore, we expect the case when γ​κ2≤1\gamma\kappa^{2}\leq 1, that is, where we get the most significant improvement other OLOP, to be the most common in practice.

The reset condition

As discussed in Section 4, in the stochastic reward case, the effect of the reset condition affects, PlaTγ\gammaPOOS as follows. First, all polynomial rates stay the same. Next, only the exponential rates change. A ρn\rho^{n} rate without the condition becomes a ρn\rho^{\sqrt{n}} with it. Next, a ρn\rho^{\sqrt{n}} rate becomes a ρn1/3\rho^{n^{1/3}} one.

6 Numerical experiments

In this section, we empirically illustrate the benefits of PlaTγ\gammaPOOS. We chose a simple MDP, shown in Figure 5. In this MDP, a state x≜(bin,d)x\triangleq({\rm bin},d) is a pair of a binary variable bin{\rm bin} and a non-negative integer dd. The MDP has two actions that are also binary. If bin≠a{\rm bin}\neq a, the base reward is 22, in which case, the next state is (a,0)(a,0). Otherwise, if bin=a,{\rm bin}=a, then r=dr=d and the next state is (a,d+1)(a,d+1). The reward is then shifted by adding 100 to it so that the noises with different ranges can be added on top without making the reward negative.

The initial state is (0,0)(0,0). Therefore, the agent has a choice. It can, for instance, remain in the same binary state bin, starting with a null reward but sees its instant reward growing with time if it keeps taking the same action in the future. Alternatively, it could greedily switch to the other binary state bin{\rm bin} and obtain a reward of 22 but delaying the hope of obtaining growing reward as in the first scenario. We set γ=0.95\gamma=0.95. Therefore, Rmax≈130R_{\max}\approx 130.

Figure 4 reports the results. All the figures show the cumulative discounted return collected by OLOP and PlaTγ\gammaPOOS after having interacted for 2020 steps with the MDP, having chosen each time an action following their planning strategy and then being transferred to the state resulting of applying the recommended action in the current state; therefore also collecting a reward that is composing the final return.

Note that the return reported are shifted in order to not take into account the fixed 100100 part of each the reward. The figures in the top row, as well as the figure at the bottom left, reports the comparison between the two returns of OLOP and PlaTγ\gammaPOOS for different ranges of noise bb. PlaTγ\gammaPOOS is systematically outperforming OLOP while in this case OLOP is given the correct R~m​a​x\widetilde{R}_{max} as input, R~m​a​x=Rmax\widetilde{R}_{max}=R_{\max} and the correct range of the noise b~,\widetilde{b}, that is b~=b\widetilde{b}=b.

In Figure 4, bottom center and right, we illustrate the sensitivity of OLOP to misleading input parameters. Notice that the performance of OLOP is very vulnerable to these misspecifications while PlaTγ\gammaPOOS is not using such inputs.

Appendix B PlaTγ\gammaPOOS is not using a budget larger than n+1n+1

Notice that for any given depth h∈[1:hmax]h\in[1:h_{\rm max}], PlaTγ\gammaPOOS never uses more evaluations than (pmax+1)​hmaxh(p_{\rm max}+1)\frac{h_{\rm max}}{h} because

∑p=0⌊log2⁡(hmax/⌈h​γ2​h⌉)⌋⌊hmaxh⁡⌈h​2p​γ2​h⌉⌋⌈h2pγ2​h⌉≤(⌊log2(hmax/⌈hγ2​h⌉)⌋+1)hmaxh⋅\displaystyle\sum_{p=0}^{\left\lfloor\log_{2}(h_{\rm max}/\left\lceil h\gamma^{2h}\right\rceil)\right\rfloor}\left\lfloor\frac{h_{\rm max}}{h\left\lceil h2^{p}\gamma^{2h}\right\rceil}\right\rfloor\left\lceil h2^{p}\gamma^{2h}\right\rceil\leq\left(\left\lfloor\log_{2}(h_{\rm max}/\left\lceil h\gamma^{2h}\right\rceil)\right\rfloor+1\right)\frac{h_{\rm max}}{h}\cdot

Summing over the depths, PlaTγ\gammaPOOS never uses more evaluations than the budget n+1n+1 during its depth exploration as

1+(pmax+1)​∑h=1hmax⌊hmaxh⌋\displaystyle 1+(p_{\rm max}+1)\sum_{h=1}^{h_{\rm max}}\left\lfloor\frac{h_{\rm max}}{h}\right\rfloor ≤1+(pmax+1)​hmax​∑h=1hmax1h\displaystyle\leq 1+(p_{\rm max}+1)h_{\rm max}\sum_{h=1}^{h_{\rm max}}\frac{1}{h}
=1+hmax​log¯​(hmax)​(pmax+1)≤1+hmax​(pmax+1)2\displaystyle=1+h_{\rm max}\overline{\log}(h_{\rm max})(p_{\rm max}+1)\leq 1+h_{\rm max}(p_{\rm max}+1)^{2}
≤n2+1.\displaystyle\leq\frac{n}{2}+1.

We need to add the additional evaluation for the cross-validation at the end,

∑p=0pmax∑t=0hmax(t+1)​γ2​t​hmax(1−γ2)2≤∑p=0pmax⌊n2​(log2⁡n+1)2⌋≤n2⋅\displaystyle\sum_{p=0}^{p_{\rm max}}\sum_{t=0}^{h_{\rm max}}\frac{(t+1)\gamma^{2t}h_{\rm max}}{(1-\gamma^{2})^{2}}\leq\sum_{p=0}^{p_{\rm max}}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2(\log_{2}n+1)^{2}}\right\rfloor\leq\frac{n}{2}\cdot

Therefore, the total budget is never more than n/2+n/2+1=n+1n/2+n/2+1=n+1. Again, notice we use the budget of n+1n+1 only for the notational convenience, we could also use n/4n/4 for the evaluation in the end to fit under nn. Nonetheless, it’s important that the amount of openings is linear in nn.

Lemma 2.

Let ξ\xi be the event under which all average estimates for the reward of the state-action pairs receiving at least one evaluation from PlaTγ\gammaPOOS are within their confidence interval, then P⁡(ξ)≥1−δP(\xi)\geq 1-\delta, where

ξ≜{∀a∈𝒞,∀0pt∈[:0pt(a)],p∈[:pmax]:if Ta[h]≥⌈(h−1)2pγ2​(h−1)⌋,then|u^(a)−u(a)|≤bpmax​log⁡(4​n/δ)2p+1}⋅\displaystyle\xi\triangleq\left\{\!\forall a\in\mathcal{C},\forall 0pt\in[2\!:\!0pt(a)],\,p\in[0\!:\!p_{\rm max}]:\text{if\ }T_{a_{[h]}}\geq\left\lceil(h-1)2^{p}\gamma^{2(h\!-\!1)}\!\right\rfloor\!,\text{then}\left|\widehat{u}(a)\!-\!u(a)\right|\leq b\sqrt{\frac{p_{\rm max}\log(4n/\delta)}{2^{p+1}}}\right\}\!\cdot

Therefore using a Azuma-Hoeffding concentration inequality with a union bound already on the values of T we have

Appendix E Use of the budget

Remark 1.

The algorithm can be made anytime and agnostic to nn using the standard doubling trick.

Remark 2 (More efficient use of the budget).

Because of the use of the floor functions ⌊⋅⌋\left\lfloor\cdot\right\rfloor, the budget used in practice can be significantly smaller than nn. While this only affects numerical constants in the bounds, in practice, it can noticeably influence the performance. Therefore one should consider, for instance, having hmaxh_{\rm max} replaced by c×hmaxc\times h_{\rm max} with cc been the largest number such that the budget is still smaller than nn. Additionally, the use of the budget nn could be slightly optimized by taking into account that the necessary number of pulls at depth hh cannot be larger than KhK^{h}.
